blocks.text: Chapter 1: Twelve Years Without a Wedding Ring
My name is Lee Bennett, and I had been married to Mark for twenty-six years.
I thought I knew every detail of my husband.
I knew he hated tomatoes but loved tomato soup. I knew he whistled when he was nervous and rubbed his left thumb against his wedding finger whenever he was worried.
And I knew he hadn’t worn his wedding band in twelve years.
He’d stopped wearing it after his father died, claiming the ring made his finger itch. I’d teased him about it for years, but eventually, I’d stopped asking.
So when he returned from his annual fishing trip with a pale, unmistakable circle around that finger, I noticed immediately.
“What’s that?” I asked, nodding toward his hand.
For a fraction of a second, something flickered across his face. Fear, perhaps. Then it disappeared.
“Fishing rod,” he said. “I’ve been gripping it for hours.”
“Since when does a fishing rod leave a ring-shaped mark?”
Instead, he carried his luggage upstairs and shut our bedroom door.
That was the first time in twenty-six years that my husband had deliberately closed a door between us without telling me why.
And somehow, I knew it wouldn’t be the last.
The following morning, Mark left early to buy groceries.
He kissed my forehead before leaving, but his lips barely touched my skin.
I watched his car disappear down the driveway.
I wasn’t proud of what I did next. I’d never searched his belongings before. But the strange mark, his evasive answer, and the tension in his eyes had planted a seed of suspicion I couldn’t ignore.
Inside, beneath a folded jacket, I found a hotel key card.
The name printed on it made my stomach tighten.

Twenty-six years earlier, Mark and I had spent three unforgettable nights there. We’d been young, broke, and ridiculously happy. We couldn’t afford the honeymoon suite, so we’d stayed in Room 814, overlooking a small courtyard filled with white roses.
I’d once told Mark that if we ever returned, I’d want that same room.
Beneath the key card was a jewelry receipt for $2,147.
The purchase description read: CUSTOM WHITE-GOLD BAND, ENGRAVING INCLUDED.
I sat on the edge of our bed, staring at the receipt until the numbers blurred.
Then I noticed an envelope tucked into the inner pocket of his fishing bag.
Inside was a photograph of a young man standing outside a hospital. He looked remarkably like Mark, except he was perhaps twenty-five years younger.
On the back, someone had written a date.
Because the young man in the photograph wasn’t Mark.
The brother my family had buried twenty-five years ago.
Chapter 3: The Brother Who Never Came Home
Daniel had disappeared when he was twenty-two.
Our family had been told he’d died in a boating accident during a storm off the coast of Maine. His body had never been recovered, but authorities eventually declared him presumed dead.
I remembered my mother collapsing into my father’s arms.
And I remembered Mark, my boyfriend at the time, holding me through the longest night of my life.
He’d helped arrange the memorial. He’d sat beside my parents through the investigation. He’d even promised my mother that he’d spend his life protecting me.
I’d always believed our marriage began in the aftermath of that tragedy.
Now I was staring at evidence suggesting my husband had been hiding something about Daniel for twenty-five years.
The photograph showed Daniel standing outside a hospital, wearing a blue sweater I’d given him for his twenty-second birthday.
And judging by the date, the photograph had been taken after the supposed accident.
My fingers found a second piece of paper folded behind it.
It was a medical document with a hospital letterhead and a signature at the bottom.
The document referenced an unidentified male patient admitted following a maritime accident.
The patient’s name had been recorded as Daniel Bennett.
But someone had crossed it out and replaced it with another name.
“Patient experiencing severe memory impairment. Family notification deferred pending psychiatric evaluation.”
I couldn’t understand what I was reading.
Why would Mark have been involved in Daniel’s hospital care?
Why would Daniel have been using another name?
And why had my husband kept this from me for twenty-five years?
Then I saw a handwritten message in the margin.
“Don’t contact Lee until we know whether the memory loss is permanent.”
Someone had made a decision about my own brother without telling me.
Someone had decided I didn’t deserve to know he was alive.
Chapter 4: The Call That Changed Everything
“Mark, where are you? What is going on? I found Daniel’s photograph.”
“Lee, you weren’t supposed to find that.”
The word was so quiet I almost didn’t hear it.
